title: Are 15 and 39 co-prime? Are 4 and 9 co-prime?
description: The factors of each number in a pair are listed and compared, and a shared factor besides one decides the pair. Keeko doubts that four and nine are co-prime, because neither is prime.
teaching_notes: One idea: two numbers are co-prime when their lists of factors share only one, and the numbers themselves need not be prime. Watch for students who mix up co-prime with prime.

source: Are 15 and 39 co-prime? Are 4 and 9 co-prime?
video_script.why: The child lists the factors of both numbers in a pair and checks whether any factor other than one is shared.
video_script.substitution: List the factors of both numbers and look for a shared factor other than one.
video_script.anchor: Two pairs of number cards with a factor list under each card
video_script.wrong_answer: four and nine are not co-prime
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko thinks four and nine are not co-prime because neither of them is prime, but co-prime depends on shared factors and the pair shares only one.
video_script.payoff_line: Fifteen and thirty nine are not co-prime, as three is a common factor. Four and nine are co-prime.

final_answer.value: 15 and 39 are not co-prime (3 is a common factor); 4 and 9 are co-prime.
final_answer.spoken: the first pair shares a factor and the second does not

maths_rules: co-prime: no common factor other than 1
factors of 15: 1, 3, 5, 15; factors of 39: 1, 3, 13, 39; 3 is shared, so not co-prime
factors of 4: 1, 2, 4; factors of 9: 1, 3, 9; only 1 is shared, so co-prime
4 and 9 are co-prime even though neither is prime
video_script.design: Each pair of cards has the two factor lists drawn below it; a shared factor other than one glows amber.
